title: SEC Institutes Settled Orders as to Seven Individuals for Operating as Unregistered Brokers that Facilitated the Offer and Sale of Security-Based Swaps
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File Nos. 3-22759; 3-22760; 3-22761; 3-22762; 3-22763; 3-22764; 3-22765 September 30, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against seven individuals for acting as unregistered brokers in the offer and sale of security-based swaps to U.S. retail investors in the form of “contracts for differences” (CFDs) based on the values of U.S. and European stocks.  The SEC’s orders find that the individuals, Quillan Black, Tyler MacKechnie, Jordan Morgan, Lewis Neal, Michael Levi Peters, Michael Talento, and Anthony Tyler Williams (collectively, the “white-label operators”), owned, operated, and marketed brokerage platforms through which third parties offered and sold and facilitated the offer and sale of security-based swaps to U.S. retail investors from 2019 through 2025. According to the SEC’s orders, the white-label operators, many of whom were prominent traders or influencers, purchased ready-to-operate white-label brokerage platforms (“white-label brokers”) from a third party to operate under their own brand and facilitate trading in CFDs. The CFDs were based on stocks, commodities, and other assets, and were offered and sold by a third party through the white-label brokers. The orders find that the white-label operators were then responsible for marketing and soliciting customer interest in trading though the white-label brokers and promoted the white-label brokers on social media and through affiliate programs. The orders also find that the white-label operators engaged in operational efforts to support the business and customer experience. According to the orders, Black and Williams co-owned and operated a broker located at www.kot4x.com; MacKechnie owned and operated a broker located at www.envifx.com; Morgan, Peters, and Talento co-owned and operated a broker located at www.prosperity4x.com; and Neal co-owned and operated a broker located at www.fxsway.com. The white-label operators were not registered with the Commission as broker-dealers and were not associated with any registered broker-dealers. The SEC’s orders find that the white-label operators violated Section 15(a)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Without admitting the SEC’s findings, the white-label operators consented to the issuance of cease-and-desist orders barring them from association with any broker, dealer, investment adviser, municipal securities dealer, municipal advisor, transfer agent, or nationally recognized statistical rating organization, with a right to apply for reentry after two years, and agreed to pay the following civil penalties: $125,000 as to each Black and Williams; $85,000 as to MacKechnie; $65,000 as to each Morgan, Peters, and Talento; and $60,000 as to Neal. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Ivan J. Snyder and Katherine Zucca with assistance from Bryan Hsueh and supervised by Erin E. Wilk and Laura D’Allaird of the Division of Enforcement’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the United Kingdom Financial Conduct Authority in this matter.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Order as to CBIZ Relating to Unregistered Offers and Sales of Securities
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22757 September 28, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today filed settled charges against CBIZ, Inc. (“CBIZ”) in connection with unregistered offers and sales of securities.  In determining to accept the CBIZ’s offer of settlement, which does not impose a civil penalty, the Commission considered the cooperation afforded to the Commission staff and remedial acts promptly undertaken by CBIZ. According to the SEC’s order, between October 16, 2023 and April 15, 2026, CBIZ sold 481,049 shares of its common stock pursuant to its 2007 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (“ESPP”) in excess of the number registered on Form S-8 registration statements.  The SEC’s order finds that CBIZ offered and sold the above-mentioned shares to its employees in violation of the registration provisions of the Securities Act of 1933, and that the violation occurred as a result of CBIZ not keeping adequate records of the aggregate amount of its open-market purchases and sales of shares pursuant to the ESPP during the relevant period. According to the SEC’s order, upon identifying that it had sold excess shares under the ESPP, CBIZ promptly suspended the ESPP and conducted an investigation.  The SEC’s order further finds that CBIZ then self-reported the violation to the Commission, voluntarily produced relevant factual information and documentation to the Commission staff, and voluntarily made a rescission offer to all affected current and former employees for all shares sold in excess of the ESPP registration.  The order finds that CBIZ violated Sections 5(a) and 5(c) of the Securities Act. Without admitting the findings in the order, CBIZ agreed to cease-and-desist from violating the charged provisions. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Nicholas Flath and Kenneth Gottlieb and supervised by Lindsay S. Moilanen and Sheldon L. Pollock, all of the SEC’s New York Regional Office.  The Enforcement Division appreciates the assistance of their colleagues from the Division of Corporation Finance.

title: SEC Charges Three Michigan Residents with Insider Trading
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File Nos. 3-22754; 3-22755; 3-22756 September 25, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Venar Ayar and Johnanthan Denha of West Bloomfield, Michigan and Vincent Ayar of Bloomfield Hills, Michigan for insider trading in advance of the August 5, 2025, announcement that Y-mAbs Therapeutics, Inc. was being acquired by SERB Pharmaceuticals through an all-cash tender offer. According to the SEC’s orders, Venar Ayar learned material nonpublic information about the Y-mAbs acquisition from his law firm partner, whose spouse worked on the acquisition for SERB, and Ayar breached his duty of trust and confidence to his law firm partner by disclosing that information to his brother, Vincent Ayar, and his cousin, Denha, and advising them to trade. As found in the orders, on August 4, 2025, Vincent Ayar purchased 1,847 shares of Y-mAbs stock, and Denha purchased 6,200 shares of Y-mAbs stock prior to the announcement. Denha also allegedly caused his cousin to buy Y-mAbs stock. On the day of the acquisition announcement, the order finds that Y-mAbs stock closed 103.34% higher than the previous day, resulting in profits of $7,831.25   for   Vincent Ayar, $25,604.65 for Denha, and $808.96 for Denha’s cousin. The SEC’s orders find that Venar Ayar, Vincent Ayar, and Denha violated the antifraud provisions of Sections 10(b) and 14(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rules 10b-5 and 14e-3(a) thereunder. Without admitting the SEC’s findings, Venar Ayar, Vincent Ayar, and Denha each consented to the issuance of a cease-and-desist order. Venar Ayar agreed to pay a civil penalty of $34,244.86; Vincent Ayar agreed to pay disgorgement of $7,831.25, prejudgment interest of $274.72, and a civil penalty of $7,831.25; and Denha agreed to pay disgorgement of $25,604.65, prejudgment interest of $898.20, and a civil penalty of $26,413.61. The actions originated from the Enforcement Division’s Market Abuse Unit (MAU) Analysis and Detection Center, which uses data analysis to detect suspicious trading patterns. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Frank Goldman, John Rymas, and Danielle Voorhees of the MAU, with the assistance of Patrick McCluskey and Darren Boerner, under the supervision of MAU Chief Joseph G. Sansone. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

title: SEC Charges Investment Adviser with Fraud for Failing to Disclose Referral Fees Obtained in Exchange for Investment Advice
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22753 September 24, 2026 – The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Keith R. Gebert, the founder, sole owner, and managing member of Rightbridge Private Capital LLC, formerly a New Jersey-registered investment adviser, for failing to disclose referral fees he received in connection with investment recommendations made to his advisory clients. The SEC’s order finds that, from October 2020 through March 2023, Gebert advised approximately 36 advisory clients to invest approximately $10 million in a private fund focused on real estate investments. According to the order, in exchange for these recommendations Gebert received more than $500,000 in referral fees from a real estate company affiliated with the fund. As stated in the order, Gebert did not disclose these fees to his clients, breaching his fiduciary duty and contradicting material representations made to those clients. Ultimately, the order finds, the real estate fund ceased all operations, and nearly all Gebert’s clients have been unable to recover their investments. The SEC’s order finds that Gebert willfully violated Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Without admitting the findings, Gebert agreed to the entry of a cease-and-desist order; to be barred from association with, among other entities, any investment adviser, broker, dealer, or investment company; to pay disgorgement of $509,350 and prejudgment interest of $135,138; and to pay a civil money penalty of $150,000. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Howard S. Kim, Samuel M. Kalar, Kenneth E. Gottlieb, and Doreen M. Rodriguez and supervised by Sandeep Satwalekar and Sheldon L. Pollock of the New York Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the New Jersey Office of the Attorney General.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Order Against Investment Adviser in Connection with a Representative’s Cancel-Rebill Scheme
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22747 September 22, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Truist Advisory Services, Inc. (“Truist Advisory”), an investment advisory firm based in Atlanta, Georgia, in connection with one of its representative’s scheme to cancel losing trades out of his personal account and rebill them to certain of his clients.  The SEC’s order finds that from March 3 to August 1, 2023, one of Truist Advisory’s representatives used its trade correction process to cancel ten losing trades from his personal brokerage account and rebill them to four of his clients.  According to the order, by cancel-rebilling those trades and their unrealized losses, the representative misappropriated $503,659 from his advisory clients.  The order finds that Truist Advisory approved the ten trade correction requests without considering that the trades were being cancel-rebilled from Costello’s personal brokerage account to certain of his clients’ accounts and without following its account trading policy to monitor for representative’s patterns of trading errors. The order finds that Truist Advisory violated the antifraud and compliance provisions of Sections 206(2) and 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder.  Without admitting the findings in the order, Truist Advisory agreed to a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and a $200,000 civil penalty. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by staff in its Los Angeles Regional Office and supervised by Robert H. Conrrad and Brent Wilner.

title: SEC Censures OTC Link LLC for Repeated Compliance Failures Related to Regulation SCI
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22748 September 22, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today censured OTC Link LLC, a New York-based broker dealer, and ordered it to pay a $575,000 civil penalty for longstanding violations of Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (SCI). According to the SEC’s settled order, between August 2016 and March 2025, OTC Link LLC failed to establish, maintain, and enforce certain written policies and procedures required by Regulation SCI for OTC Link ATS—an Alternative Trading System for over-the-counter securities that it operates—including policies and procedures pertaining to system security, access control, and application vulnerability management, testing, and remediation. Although staff in the SEC’s Division of Examinations examined OTC Link ATS several times during the relevant period and each time flagged certain required policies and procedures that the firm had not established or kept in draft form and failed to finalize or enforce, the SEC’s order finds that OTC Link LLC repeatedly failed to promptly remediate such deficiencies. The SEC’s order finds that OTC Link LLC lacked written policies and procedures that were reasonably designed to ensure that OTC Link ATS’s SCI systems and, for purposes of security standards, indirect SCI systems, had levels of capacity, integrity, resiliency, availability, and security, adequate to maintain OTC Link ATS’s operational capability and promote the maintenance of fair and orderly markets in violation of Rule 1001(a)(1) of Regulation SCI. By failing to have required minimum policies and procedures, to periodically review the effectiveness of its policies and procedures, and to take prompt action to remedy its deficiencies, the SEC’s order also finds that OTC Link LLC violated Rules 1001(a)(2) and 1001(a)(3). Without admitting the findings, OTC Link LLC agreed to a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and a civil penalty of $575,000. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Adam Gottlieb and supervised by Paul Kim and Laura D’Allaird of the Division of Enforcement’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Order as to Investment Adviser and Its Principal for Breach of Fiduciary Duties
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22735 September 18, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today filed settled administrative and cease-and-desist proceedings against Hatteras Investment Partners, LP, a North Carolina-based registered investment adviser, and its principal, David B. Perkins, for recommending a high-risk liquidation transaction in breach of their fiduciary duties to their clients. According to the SEC’s order, in 2021, Perkins and Hatteras recommended a transaction to the Board of Directors of several registered funds (“the funds”) after the Board had asked Hatteras to explore liquidation options with the goal of distributing all proceeds to shareholders.  The order explains that the recommended transaction, which the Board approved, involved the funds exchanging their entire portfolios of illiquid, alternative assets for preferred shares of Beneficient—a former private startup that purported to offer liquidity solutions to holders of alternative assets, selling their preferred shares upon Beneficient’s contemplated initial public offering, and distributing the cash to the shareholders. The order finds that Perkins and Hatteras ignored multiple red flags associated with Beneficient that arose during the due diligence process and that they did not understand the terms of the transaction or that it would not achieve the Board’s goals or allow the funds’ shareholders to recoup their investments in the funds.  The order further states that Perkins conducted due diligence on the transaction almost entirely on his own and that he ignored advice from Hatteras’s Fractional CFO not to follow through with the transaction.  According to the order, when Beneficient eventually went public through a SPAC merger in 2023, its shares plummeted in value, resulting in losses of approximately $300 million to the funds.  The order finds that Perkins and Hatteras did not have a reasonable basis to conclude that the transaction would be in the funds’ best interest and provide either the liquidity the funds were seeking for shareholders or a path to liquidate and terminate the funds. The order finds that Hatteras and Perkins willfully violated Section 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting the order’s findings, Hatteras and Perkins agreed to a cease-and-desist order and censures, and Perkins agreed to pay a civil penalty of $250,000. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Katie Shelton with assistance from H.B. Roback and Krysta Cannon, and supervised by Matt McNamara and Justin Jeffries, all of the SEC’s Atlanta Regional Office.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Order as to Long Island Investment Adviser and its Principal for Fee Overcharges and Improper Registration with the Commission
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22734 September 18, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Pursino Advisory Group (“PAG”), an investment adviser formerly registered with the Commission, and against Philip Pursino, PAG’s sole owner and operator, for overcharging clients and failing to timely deregister PAG’s business.  According to the order, from January 2020 to March 31, 2023, Pursino and PAG overbilled 28 advisory clients by $53,984.64.  The order finds that PAG and Pursino charged advisory fees above the fees set out in PAG’s Form ADV and agreed to by its clients, and Pursino and PAG charged one client $22,078.69 in fees on cash assets that were not managed by PAG.  Additionally, the order finds that PAG was improperly registered with the Commission from at least June 30, 2023, until it withdrew its registration on June 28, 2024, because it did not have sufficient Regulatory Assets Under Management (“RAUM”).  As a New York-based investment adviser, PAG was generally prohibited from registering with the Commission unless it managed at least $25 million, according to the order.  The SEC’s order finds that PAG and Pursino willfully violated Section 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and that PAG willfully violated, and Pursino caused PAG’s violations of, Advisers Act Section 203A and Rule 203A-1 thereunder, which prohibit an investment adviser from registering with the Commission unless the adviser meets certain eligibility requirements.  Without admitting the SEC’s findings, PAG and Pursino consented to a cease-and-desist order and a censure. In addition, PAG and Pursino agreed to pay civil penalties of $25,000 and $15,000, respectively.  The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Dina Levy and was supervised by Janna Berke and Sheldon Pollock, all of the SEC’s New York Regional Office. The team was assisted by Cynthia Chin, John Bulla, Merryl Hoffman, and George DeAngelis of the Division of Examinations.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Orders for Insider Trading in Advance of Okta Earnings Announcement
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22722, 3-22723 September 15, 2026 – The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Andrew T. Neller of South Lyon, Michigan and Jack E. Alexander of Rescue, California for insider trading in advance of Okta, Inc.’s August 31, 2022 announcement that it was lowering its guidance for a key non-GAAP metric. According to the SEC’s orders, on August 4, 2022, Neller, then an Okta employee, attended a confidential, companywide meeting and learned that Okta’s internal financial plan for the year was wrong, too optimistic, and needed to be adjusted. The orders also find that Neller learned that Okta was suffering significant attrition in its sales force and having difficulty integrating a recently-acquired company. The orders further find that on August 30, 2022, Neller purchased Okta put options. The next day, according to the orders, Neller warned Alexander, his friend and former Okta colleague, that Okta would likely be lowering its financial guidance, and Neller also advised Alexander to buy Okta put options. The orders find that after receiving these messages, Alexander sold all his Okta stock and purchased Okta put options. The orders further find that, after the markets closed on August 31, 2022, Okta announced that it was lowering its full-year guidance for calculated billings. According to the orders, the next day, September 1, Okta’s stock price declined 34%, and Neller and Alexander sold all the put options they had bought. The orders find that Neller and Alexander realized profits of $98,754.00 and $170,859.52, respectively, and that Alexander also avoided losses of $59,381.78. The SEC’s orders find that Neller and Alexander violated Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. Without admitting the SEC’s findings, Neller and Alexander each consented to the issuance of a cease-and-desist order against them. Neller agreed to pay disgorgement of $98,754.00, prejudgment interest of $13,817.65, and a civil penalty of $328,995.30. Alexander agreed to pay disgorgement of $230,241.30, prejudgment interest of $32,215.35, and a civil penalty of $230,241.30. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Matthew Meyerhofer and supervised by Christina Filipp and Jason H. Lee, all of the SEC’s San Francisco Regional Office.

title: SEC Institutes Settled Order for Insider Trading Charges Related to Acquisition of Kimball International
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22721 September 15, 2026 –  The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against Gregory Dale Smith of McCormick, South Carolina for insider trading in advance of the June 1, 2023 acquisition of Kimball International, Inc. by HNI Corporation. According to the SEC’s order, Smith learned about the impending acquisition from his brother, who is married to a Kimball executive. The order finds (i) that Smith’s brother told him about the impending acquisition in trust and confidence, told him that this information was non-public and specifically instructed Smith not to trade on it; and (ii) that Smith knew or was reckless in not knowing that his brother learned the information in confidence from the Kimball executive. According to the order, Smith breached the duty of trust and confidence he owed to his brother by purchasing 11,455 shares of Kimball stock between February 10 and February 27, 2023. The order finds that Smith then sold those shares after the merger was announced and obtained profits of $59,710.85. The SEC’s order finds that Smith violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. Without admitting the findings, Smith consented to the issuance of a cease-and-desist order and agreed to pay disgorgement of $59,710.85, prejudgment interest of $14,728.45, and a civil money penalty of $59,710.85, for a total of $134,150.15. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Joe Burson, with assistance from Bob Nesbitt of the Division of Enforcement’s Office of Investigative and Market Analytics and Mathew Wong of the Division’s Market Abuse Unit. The investigation was supervised by Jeff Leasure, D. Mark Cave, and Michael Brennan. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

title: SEC Charges California Registered Investment Adviser with Failing to Report Certain Securities Holdings
text: ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING File No. 3-22707 September 8, 2026 – The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced settled charges against dually registered investment adviser and broker dealer Independent Financial Group, LLC for failing to file reports, known as Forms 13F, that it was required to file because it has investment discretion over more than $100 million in certain reportable securities. According to the order, since at least December 2021, Independent Financial Group, LLC, an institutional investment manager as defined in Section 13(f) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, has had investment discretion pursuant to Rule 13f-1(b) over at least $100 million of reportable securities and was therefore obligated to file quarterly Forms 13F beginning by at least February 2022. As alleged in the order, throughout this time, Independent Financial Group, LLC’s Chief Compliance Officers recommended that the company file Forms 13F, however, no Forms 13F were filed until May 2026. As such, the order finds that Independent Financial Group, LLC willfully violated Section 13(f)(1) of the Exchange Act and Rule 13f-1 thereunder. Without admitting the findings, Independent Financial Group, LLC has agreed to a cease and desist order, a censure, and a $500,000 civil penalty. The SEC’s investigation was conducted by Jennifer Turner under the supervision of Kimberly Frederick and Nicholas Heinke of the SEC’s Denver Regional Office. More information about Forms 13F is available at Form 13F - Reports Filed by Institutional Investment Managers | Investor.gov
